input.question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?
input.ground_truth: Chess is a unique game, in that each piece has only certain moves that can be performed at any time, and thus one can predict which moves will be done many turns in advance, and each move to counter them. There is really no "randomness" in chance. This allows a computer to be programmed to constantly monitor the positions of each piece on the board, and do exactly that, think 10+ turns ahead and figure out each counterplay to each possible movement of each piece on the board, your own and your opponents. & #x200B; It's very close to what a grandmaster in chess does, however, a computer is not subject to stress or other interferences.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine a robot that plays chess. At first, the robot only knows the rules, like how each piece moves. But it doesn’t know which moves are good or bad.

People play with the robot a lot. Every time the robot makes a good move, they say “good job!” and when it makes a bad move, they say “uh-oh.” The robot remembers these lessons and learns which moves help it win.

Later, people made the robot read many, many chess books and watch lots of games. The robot practiced playing chess with itself over and over, trying different moves and seeing what works best.

Now, the robot can look ahead and think, “If I move my knight here, and you move your pawn there, then I can do this!” It can think many moves ahead, just like a smart grown-up.

That’s how computers got so good at playing chess—they practiced a lot and learned from many games! 🤖♟️
